new_entry.title: Scuderia Ferrari is founded
new_entry.subtitle: A racing team before a car manufacturer
new_entry.summary: Enzo Ferrari founded Scuderia Ferrari in Modena on 16 November 1929, initially racing Alfa Romeo cars.
body: Scuderia Ferrari was founded in Modena on 16 November 1929, with Enzo Ferrari as its director. Its purpose was to acquire Alfa Romeo cars and enter motor races with experienced drivers: the team came before the cars that would bear Ferrari's own name. Its first racing appearance was the 1930 Mille Miglia, where its entries retired. In 1933, Alfa Romeo entrusted the Scuderia with managing its racing activities. The relationship gave Ferrari's Modena operation increasing independence and a role in developing competition cars. The date shown here marks the racing team's foundation, rather than the later birth of Ferrari as a car manufacturer.
story_headings: A racing team before a car manufacturer
new_entry.date_reference: Foundation of Società Anonima Scuderia Ferrari in Modena, 16 November 1929; not Enzo Ferrari's birth or the 1947 Ferrari car debut.

new_entry.title: The first 24 Hours of Le Mans
new_entry.subtitle: Speed tested against time and reliability
new_entry.summary: The first 24 Hours of Le Mans took place on 26–27 May 1923, testing the endurance of touring cars.
body: The first 24 Hours of Le Mans began on 26 May 1923 and finished the following day. Conceived by Georges Durand, Charles Faroux and Émile Coquille, the event offered a different test from a short contest of outright speed: touring cars had to keep running through an entire day and night. Thirty-three cars started on the roads around Le Mans. André Lagache and René Léonard, sharing the number 9 Chenard & Walcker, completed 128 laps and more than 2,200 kilometres to head the inaugural result. The race made reliability, teamwork and endurance central to its identity. Its date here is the start of the first edition, not the establishment of its organising club.
story_headings: Speed tested against time and reliability
new_entry.date_reference: Start of the inaugural race, 26 May 1923; the race ended on 27 May.

new_entry.title: Football begins to share one code
new_entry.subtitle: The Football Association and common rules
new_entry.summary: The Football Association was formed in London on 26 October 1863 to establish a common set of football rules.
body: On 26 October 1863, representatives of London and suburban football clubs met at the Freemasons' Tavern to form the Football Association. Clubs and schools already played many different versions of football; the problem was agreeing how opponents should play together. Ebenezer Morley helped bring them together around a common written code. Further meetings that autumn settled the Association's laws, separating its game from versions that permitted carrying the ball and hacking opponents' legs. This was a decisive step in the development of association football, rather than the invention of every game played with a ball and feet. The date marks the Association's first meeting, not the adoption of today's complete rulebook.
story_headings: The Football Association and common rules
new_entry.date_reference: The Football Association's founding meeting, 26 October 1863. Codification continued through further meetings that autumn.

new_entry.title: Naismith invents basketball
new_entry.subtitle: An indoor game for a New England winter
new_entry.summary: James Naismith devised basketball in Springfield in December 1891; its first game is commemorated on 21 December.
body: In December 1891, James Naismith devised basketball at the International YMCA Training School, now Springfield College, in Massachusetts. His supervisor, Luther Gulick, wanted an engaging indoor activity for the winter. Naismith combined a football with two peach baskets fixed above the floor and thirteen rules. The first players formed two teams of nine; running while holding the ball was forbidden, so passing was essential. The first game is commemorated on 21 December 1891, and the rules appeared in the school's magazine in January 1892. Students helped carry the new sport to other places. Later changes introduced features such as dribbling and open-bottomed nets; the familiar modern game did not appear fully formed that day.
story_headings: An indoor game for a New England winter
new_entry.date_reference: Traditional first-game date, 21 December 1891, recognised by the Basketball Hall of Fame and FIBA; invention occurred that December.

new_entry.title: The Knickerbocker baseball rules
new_entry.subtitle: A developing game finds a written framework
new_entry.summary: The New York Knickerbocker club compiled baseball rules in 1845, an important stage in a much older game's development.
body: In 1845, New York's Knickerbocker Base Ball Club compiled a written set of rules that became influential in baseball's development. They distinguished fair and foul ground, prohibited putting runners out by throwing the ball at them, and provided for three outs before changing sides. A notable match under these rules was played at Elysian Fields in Hoboken on 19 June 1846. The game still differed from today's baseball: pitching was underhand and a contest could be played to twenty-one runs rather than nine innings. These documents mark a stage in an evolving bat-and-ball tradition, not a single person's invention. The familiar tale that Abner Doubleday invented baseball in Cooperstown in 1839 has been refuted.
story_headings: A developing game finds a written framework
new_entry.date_reference: Compilation of the Knickerbocker rules in 1845; June 19, 1846 is a subsequent match, not the date assigned to this entry.

new_entry.title: Rugby School writes its football laws
new_entry.subtitle: Written laws beyond a founding legend
new_entry.summary: Pupils at Rugby School drew up written football laws in 1845, a documented milestone in rugby's development.
body: In 1845, three Rugby School pupils drew up the first written football laws associated with their school's game. Printed in a pocket-sized book, the code helped define a form of play that former pupils carried to universities and clubs. Terms including the try became part of its vocabulary. This documented milestone should be distinguished from the famous story that William Webb Ellis picked up a ball and ran with it in 1823. That story is a tradition whose historical validity has been questioned, not a securely witnessed moment of invention. Rugby developed through school practices, written rules and later organisations, rather than a single dramatic gesture. The date here refers to the 1845 code.
story_headings: Written laws beyond a founding legend
new_entry.date_reference: The 1845 written Rugby School code; not the disputed Webb Ellis story of 1823 or the later Rugby Football Union.

new_entry.title: Organised ice hockey moves indoors
new_entry.subtitle: A scheduled match at Montreal's Victoria Rink
new_entry.summary: James Creighton organised a public indoor ice-hockey match at Montreal's Victoria Skating Rink on 3 March 1875.
body: On 3 March 1875, Montreal's Victoria Skating Rink hosted an organised indoor ice-hockey match arranged by James George Aylwin Creighton. Two named teams of nine players faced each other before spectators, using a flattened wooden disc. Creighton's side beat Charles Torrance's team by two goals to one. A newspaper announcement before the match and a report afterwards gave the event a public record. Games with sticks and balls on ice already existed elsewhere; this was not the first time people had ever played on frozen ground. Its importance lay in bringing a scheduled contest, fixed teams and spectators together indoors, helping establish the organised sport that developed further in Montreal.
story_headings: A scheduled match at Montreal's Victoria Rink
new_entry.date_reference: The documented organised indoor match at the Victoria Skating Rink, 3 March 1875; not the invention of all earlier ice-and-stick games.

new_entry.title: Rutgers and Princeton play collegiate football
new_entry.subtitle: A starting point, before the modern gridiron game
new_entry.summary: Rutgers beat Princeton on 6 November 1869 in a collegiate football match whose rules were closer to association football than today's American football.
body: Rutgers and Princeton met in New Brunswick, New Jersey, on 6 November 1869 in the match traditionally recognised as the beginning of intercollegiate American football. Rutgers won six goals to four, with twenty-five players on each side. The agreed rules drew on London's Football Association code: players kicked or batted the ball rather than carrying it as in the modern gridiron game. Calling it a starting point does not mean that today's sport already existed. Later changes, including those promoted by Walter Camp, introduced defining features such as eleven-player teams, a line of scrimmage and a system of downs. The date identifies this particular collegiate match within that longer evolution.
story_headings: A starting point, before the modern gridiron game
new_entry.date_reference: Rutgers–Princeton collegiate match, 6 November 1869; soccer-style rules preceded the later development of American football under Walter Camp and others.

new_entry.title: Einstein: the 1921 Nobel Prize, awarded in 1922
new_entry.subtitle: Light in discrete packets
new_entry.summary: Einstein received the reserved 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics in 1922, especially for his explanation of the photoelectric effect.
body: Albert Einstein was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for 1921 one year later, in 1922, after the committee had reserved the prize. The citation singled out the law of the photoelectric effect, rather than relativity. In his 1905 explanation, light transfers energy in discrete packets: increasing its frequency can release electrons from a material when simply making lower-frequency light brighter cannot. The award recognized a contribution to the emerging quantum description of nature. Einstein was travelling in Asia during the Stockholm ceremony in December 1922; the prize year, award year and ceremony should therefore not be mistaken for the date of his original discovery.

new_entry.title: Martin Luther King Jr. wins the Nobel Peace Prize
new_entry.subtitle: Nonviolence on the world stage
new_entry.summary: The Nobel Peace Prize announced on 14 October 1964 recognized King’s nonviolent struggle for civil rights.
body: On 14 October 1964, Martin Luther King Jr. was named the Nobel Peace Prize laureate for his nonviolent struggle for African American civil rights. The award brought international recognition to a movement built through marches, boycotts and organized resistance to segregation. King was thirty-five, then the youngest recipient of the Peace Prize. He accepted the award in Oslo on 10 December, describing it as recognition of the wider movement rather than a personal achievement alone. The announcement belongs to the same year as the United States Civil Rights Act, but it was a separate event: neither the legislation nor the Nobel Prize ended the struggle for equality.

new_entry.title: Mandela and de Klerk share the Nobel Peace Prize
new_entry.subtitle: An unfinished transition
new_entry.summary: The 1993 Nobel Peace Prize recognized Nelson Mandela and F. W. de Klerk’s work toward ending apartheid peacefully.
body: On 15 October 1993, the Nobel Peace Prize was announced jointly for Nelson Mandela and South African president F. W. de Klerk. The committee recognized their work toward a peaceful end to apartheid and the foundations of a democratic South Africa. Mandela had been released from prison in February 1990; negotiations were now moving the country toward its first democratic national election based on universal adult suffrage. The prize did not mark an already completed transition: political violence and difficult negotiations continued. Mandela’s election and inauguration as president followed in 1994, making the 1993 Nobel a distinct milestone on that road.

new_entry.title: Malala and Satyarthi win the Nobel Peace Prize
new_entry.subtitle: Education is a right
new_entry.summary: Malala Yousafzai and Kailash Satyarthi were jointly awarded the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize for defending children’s rights and education.
body: The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced Malala Yousafzai and Kailash Satyarthi as joint Peace Prize laureates on 10 October 2014. Their campaigns confronted different barriers to childhood: Malala defended girls’ access to education in Pakistan, while Satyarthi worked against the exploitation of children in India. Malala had survived a Taliban attack in 2012 and continued speaking publicly for education. At seventeen, she became the youngest Nobel laureate. Sharing the award connected two campaigns across national and religious boundaries, placing the rights of children, rather than a single personality, at the centre of its message.

new_entry.title: Bob Dylan wins the Nobel Prize in Literature
new_entry.subtitle: A song can carry literature
new_entry.summary: On 13 October 2016 the Swedish Academy awarded Bob Dylan the Nobel Prize in Literature for his contribution to the American song tradition.
body: On 13 October 2016, the Swedish Academy named Bob Dylan the recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature. Its motivation focused on the new poetic expression he had created within the American song tradition. Rather than singling out an album or a performance, the award recognized a body of work shaped through words, voice and music. The decision placed songwriting within an international literary honour usually associated in public imagination with novels, plays and poetry on the page. Dylan’s Nobel therefore concerns the literary possibilities of song; it is not a separate music prize or an award for sales.

new_entry.title: Tokyo Disneyland opens
new_entry.subtitle: Disney’s first park outside the United States
new_entry.summary: Tokyo Disneyland opened in Urayasu, Chiba, on 15 April 1983, becoming the first Disney theme park outside the United States.
body: Tokyo Disneyland opened on a rainy 15 April 1983 in Urayasu, Chiba, beside Tokyo Bay. It was the first Disney theme park outside the United States, developed by Oriental Land through an agreement with Disney. Construction had taken two years and four months; training and preview visits preceded the public opening. President Masatomo Takahashi welcomed the first guests in World Bazaar. The park carried Disney’s model of themed streets, attractions and hospitality into a new national setting, and its success became an important reference for later international expansion. Tokyo DisneySea, which opened nearby in 2001, is a separate park and a later milestone.

new_entry.subtitle: Euro Disneyland welcomes its first visitors
new_entry.summary: Euro Disneyland opened to the public at Marne-la-Vallée, east of Paris, on 12 April 1992.
body: Euro Disneyland opened to the public on 12 April 1992 at Marne-la-Vallée, east of Paris, following a weekend of previews and opening celebrations. The resort began with one theme park, hotels and an entertainment district then called Festival Disney. It was Disney’s first theme-park resort in Europe, following the international expansion already demonstrated by Tokyo Disneyland. A 1987 agreement with French authorities had established the project’s framework, with construction beginning in 1988. The destination later became known as Disneyland Paris. Its 1992 opening should not be confused with the addition of the second theme park, Walt Disney Studios Park, in 2002.

new_entry.summary: Tokyo DisneySea opened on 4 September 2001 as a separate, sea-themed park beside Tokyo Disneyland.
body: Tokyo DisneySea opened at 8 a.m. on 4 September 2001, with its inauguration taking place at Mediterranean Harbor. Rather than repeat Tokyo Disneyland, Oriental Land and Disney developed a second park around maritime journeys and imagined ports. Plans for another park had been announced in 1988; a sea-based concept emerged in 1992, and the DisneySea name was presented in 1997. The entrance’s AquaSphere became a symbol of Earth as a water planet after discussions between the Japanese and American partners. DisneySea’s opening expanded the area into a destination with two distinct parks, not a replacement for the Disneyland that had opened in 1983.

new_entry.title: 3D television enters the living room
new_entry.subtitle: Depth through two different images
new_entry.summary: In 2010, consumer 3D televisions brought stereoscopic films and games into the home through compatible screens, content and glasses.
body: In 2010, major television manufacturers promoted stereoscopic viewing as a new home-entertainment format. Sony’s BRAVIA range, for example, paired high-refresh-rate screens with active-shutter glasses, alternately showing different images to the left and right eyes to create an impression of depth. Some models included the glasses and transmitter, while others required separate accessories. Compatible films, players and broadcasts were needed alongside the television; Sony also announced PlayStation 3 updates for stereoscopic games and Blu-ray 3D playback. This was a consumer rollout of an older optical principle, not the invention of three-dimensional imaging, and the exact launch dates varied by model and market.

old_entry.summary: The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence was a 1956 summer workshop widely considered to be the founding event of artificial intelligence as a field.
body:
The Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence was a 1956 summer workshop widely considered to be the founding event of artificial intelligence as a field. The workshop has been referred to as "the Constitutional Convention of AI". The project's four organizers, Claude Shannon, John McCarthy, Nathaniel Rochester and Marvin Minsky, are considered some of the "founding fathers" of AI. However it was not the first conference devoted to what would now be described as the question of artificial intelligence: it postdated meetings such as the 1951 Paris cybernetics conference and the Macy meetings.

The project lasted approximately six to eight weeks and consisted largely of brainstorming sessions. Eleven mathematicians and scientists originally planned to attend; not all of them attended, but more than ten others came for short times.

new_entry.title: Italy's Years of Lead
new_entry.subtitle: Political terrorism and a democracy under pressure
new_entry.summary: The Years of Lead (Italian: Anni di piombo) were a period of social and political turmoil in Italy that lasted from the late 1960s to the late 1980s, marked by a wave of both far-left and far-right political terrorism.
body: The Years of Lead (Italian: Anni di piombo) were a period of social and political turmoil in Italy that lasted from the late 1960s to the late 1980s, marked by a wave of both far-left and far-right political terrorism.

Major attacks of the period include the 1969 Piazza Fontana bombing, the 1974 Piazza della Loggia bombing, and the 1980 Bologna Massacre, all committed by neo-fascist or far-right groups. Meanwhile, the 1978 kidnapping and murder of former prime minister Aldo Moro by the Red Brigades left a lasting impact on and stunned the nation. The deadliest single attack of the era was the 1980 Bologna Massacre conducted by the neo-fascist Nuclei Armati Rivoluzionari, which killed 85 people. Between 1968 and 1988, the conflict resulted in 428 deaths and approximately 2,000 injuries attributed to political violence.

new_entry.title: Genocide in Gaza
new_entry.subtitle: Civilian devastation and international accountability
new_entry.summary: The Gaza genocide is the ongoing, intentional, and systematic destruction of the Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip carried out by Israel during the Gaza war.
body: The Gaza genocide is the ongoing, intentional, and systematic destruction of the Palestinian people in the Gaza Strip carried out by Israel during the Gaza war. It encompasses mass killings, the targeted killing of children (who account for 30% of those killed), deliberate starvation, infliction of serious bodily and mental harm, and prevention of births. Other acts include blockading, destroying civilian infrastructure, destroying healthcare facilities, killing healthcare workers and aid-seekers, causing mass forced displacement, committing sexual violence, and destroying educational, religious, and cultural sites.

The genocide has been recognized, in either a legal or scholarly sense, by a United Nations special committee and commission of inquiry, the International Association of Genocide Scholars, multiple human rights groups, state governments, numerous genocide studies and international law scholars, and other experts.

new_entry.title: V for Vendetta
new_entry.summary: James McTeigue adapts Alan Moore and David Lloyd's comic into a dystopian thriller about fear, propaganda and resistance.
body: V for Vendetta is a 2006 dystopian thriller directed by James McTeigue, adapted by Lana and Lilly Wachowski from Alan Moore and David Lloyd's comic. In a future Britain ruled through fear and surveillance, Evey, played by Natalie Portman, encounters Hugo Weaving's masked insurgent V.

V turns resistance into public theatre: a broadcast interrupts official propaganda, the Guy Fawkes mask conceals his identity, and the fifth of November gives his campaign a deadline. Evey's growing involvement places a personal story inside the struggle over who controls the country's images, voices and memory.
